newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: Kazakh minister sees economic growth in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Kazakh minister sees economic growth in 1997.

text.p: Kazakhstan's finance minister on Friday declared the country had achieved economic stability in 1996 with a small increase in industrial output and said he expected the trend to continue this year.
"Tighter budget and monetary policies pursued last year resulted in a better economic performance," Finance Minister and Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Pavlov told a news conference.
Pavlov noted industrial output grew last year by 0.3 percent against a 7.9-percent fall in 1995 and he forecast a two percent increase this year.
The minister did not give figures for gross domestic product (GDP) last year, but said he expected it to grow this year to 1.74 trillion tenge ($23 billion) from 1.41 trillion in 1996.

Official figures in November said GDP for the first nine months was 1.1 percent higher than a year earlier. Pavlov said last year's deficit did not exceed 2.8 percent of GDP, below an initial target of three percent.
The 1997 budget envisages a 3.16 percent deficit in the former Soviet republic, and Pavlov said he was confident the gap would not exceed that.
Annual inflation fell to 28.7 percent from 60.3 percent in 1996, and is expected to ease further to 21 percent this year.
The drop in inflation and budget deficit were achieved largely due to developments in the state securities market.
"In 1996 the government launched issues of 12-month Treasury bills (GKOs) which turned out to be a success," Pavlov said.
Foreigners can buy 10 to 20 percent of GKO issues and last year they invested some 800 million tenge on three-, six- and 12-month paper, attracted by annual yields of some 30 percent.
The government is planning to issue two-year GKOs in the second or third quarter of this year and increase the percentage of state security issues which foreigners can buy.
"Foreigners' participation in GKO auctions will rise fairly quickly," Pavlov promised.
He also noted that the Central Asian state was granted a sovereign credit rating and appeared on international financial markets last year.
Kazakhstan won a BB minus rating from Standard & Poor's before its debut Eurobond issue in December. Foreign investors snapped up the $200-million issue, twice the placement originally planned.
Pavlov, repeating earlier comments from officials, said Kazakhstan could this year issue Samurai bonds -- bonds deonominated in yen that are issued in Japan.
"We have had interesting offers from Daewoo Securities and Namura Securities...But we pursue a balanced policy, and everything will depend on conditions we are offered," he said.

Urgent measures were being taken to form a viable stock market this year and Pavlov said shares of "large and promising local companies" would be offered to foreigners keen to invest in the resource-rich country. ($1=75.60 tenge)
